raw_response.country: Afghanistan, Bhutan, China, India, Nepal, Pakistan (Hindu Kush Himalaya region)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban drinking water supply and sanitation pressures across cities and towns in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH), including municipal water deficits, household coverage gaps, intermittent supply, and reliance on water tankers and wells.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper arguably touches on governance, regulatory, and policy issues in passing (e.g., weak urban water governance, institutional silos, un-enforced groundwater abstraction rules in municipal bye-laws, and artificially low water pricing). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it fails Criterion 2 (c2 = no) because governance is treated only as unanalysed macro-governance background and broad resource-management policy recommendations rather than an analysis of a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it contains no empirical evidence or systematic synthesis (fails c3 and c5).
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05): This is a narrative policy overview and perspective paper with no methods section, no primary data collection, no empirical analytical design, and no systematic review methodology; it compiles secondary statistics and literature across HKH towns and concludes with 12 general policy recommendations.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports secondary descriptive statistics relevant to urban water availability, coverage, continuity, and cost (e.g., Table 1 city-level MLD supply vs. demand deficits, <20% municipal supply coverage in Kabul, 2 hours/day supply in Dharamshala, and high tanker prices), though not empirically linked to a studied exposure.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not provide an identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or defined exposure-outcome evaluation because it is a non-empirical narrative overview.

evidence_quotes.quote: In order to build a holistic perspective, the paper is divided into three parts: the first part focuses on major urban centres and their water issues, followed by key issues and main challenges and issues facing urban water governance across selected case studies. We conclude with a number of recommendations concerning future strategies and actions that need to be taken to strengthen urban climate resilience in the region.

Data from 2013 indicate that, currently, Afghanistan Urban Water Supply and Sewerage Company (AUWSSC) is able to provide 15 Lpcd of water, which is only able to supply less than 20% of its population (Mukherjee et al., 2006).

Ground water abstraction policies exist in municipal bye-laws in many cases, however they are seldom followed (Quetta, Kabul, Dehradun, Haldwani), and illegal borewells and overexploitation of groundwater resources remains a problem.

The cost at which water is supplied through tankers in most cases is extremely high, hence only the affluent members of the population are able to pay the premium. The poor and vulnerable are left at the mercy of government supply which is also not equitably distributed.
Institutional capacities and urban governance mechanisms to manage water are generally low and poor.

In addition, under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2, it treats governance only as unanalysed macro-governance background and high-level policy recommendations rather than examining a rule-type mechanism governing service access (c2 = no); under the plain wording of Criterion 2 it would still be excluded for lack of empirical evidence.
